Why most beginners lose money

In Europe, every regulated broker must show on its website how many of its ordinary (retail) clients lose money trading CFDs such as forex and Gold. When the European regulator ESMA reviewed these numbers in 2018, they ranged from 74% to 89% of retail accounts losing money. So the useful question is not why so many people lose. It is: what do the people who survive do differently? This lesson answers that question and gives you the full map of the free course.

The biggest beginner mistake: the wrong order

Most beginners watch a strategy in some video, open an account and deposit money. That is like building the roof of a house before the foundation. They cannot calculate a pip, do not know lot size and do not understand leverage. Every professional trader knows that the real difference comes less from the strategy and more from risk management and discipline. The problem is not intelligence. It is the order.

Who this course is for

  • People who know nothing about forex.
  • People who have traded, lost money, and now want to learn the basics properly.

It is for viewers in Pakistan and India, in simple Urdu/Hindi, with English subtitles on every video and written notes on this website.

lessons.notes:
Can $100 really make 10% a day?

You have probably seen the claim: invest $100 and earn 10% profit every day. Let's do the maths. If $100 grew by 10% a day and you reinvested the profit every day, after 30 days it would be about $1,744.94. After a full year the number would be bigger than all the personal wealth in the world. This is only a maths illustration, not a possible trading result. If it were that easy, everyone would be rich. So how is money really made in forex, and how is it lost?

Who is in the forex market?

About $9.6 trillion of currency changes hands every day (BIS Triennial Survey 2025). Six kinds of players share that market:

PlayerWho they areWhy they trade
Big banksThe heart of the market. They quote buy and sell prices all day.Profit from the spread and their own trading
Central banksFor example the State Bank of Pakistan or the Bank of Japan.Manage their own currency, not profit
Big institutionsHedge funds, investment funds and smaller banks; roughly half of all trading.Profit
Import and export companiesBuy and sell currency to pay for goods.Protect their business (hedging), not profit
Brokers and liquidity providersConnect ordinary traders to the big market.Spread, commission, swap, and sometimes your loss
Retail traders (us)Only a few percent of the whole market.Profit, but we are the smallest fish

How powerful is a central bank? On 15 January 2015 the Swiss National Bank removed its cap on the franc with one announcement. Within minutes the Swiss franc jumped about 30%. Many retail accounts were wiped out in a single day, and a London broker went bankrupt. Retail traders like us are the smallest fish in this ocean, which is why we learn to protect ourselves first.

How to earn money from forex trading: where profit comes from

In forex, money is made from the price difference. You buy EUR/USD and the price goes up: profit. It goes down: loss. If you sell, it is the opposite. (Lesson 1.1: What is forex trading? explains buy and sell from zero.)

On the other side of every trade there is someone: another trader, a bank or liquidity provider, or your own broker. One single person does not lose exactly what you win every time, but across the whole market money is not created out of thin air; it moves from one hand to another. So a winner's money comes from two places:

  1. The losses of traders who lose.
  2. Players who trade for their needs, not for profit, such as companies and central banks.

Your profit is not a gift from the market. It came out of someone's pocket, so to win you must make better decisions than others.

Where losers' money goes: 4 places

Where it goesHowRead more
1. Fees: spread, commission, swapThe spread puts every trade slightly in minus the moment it opens. Commission applies on some account types. Swap is charged (or sometimes paid) for holding a trade overnight.What is spread · What is swap
2. The broker itselfMany brokers do not send every trade to the big market; they take the other side themselves (often called a B-book). Then your loss becomes the broker's profit. This does not mean every broker cheats, but you should know it.Forex brokers guide
3. Better traders and institutionsBanks, funds and disciplined traders with better information, tools and risk control.Risk management
4. Outside the market: scams and signal sellersPaid signal groups, account managers and "guaranteed profit" schemes take money before a single trade is placed.Signal groups · Is forex a scam?

Islamic (swap-free) accounts

Many brokers offer an Islamic or swap-free account with no swap. But most of them charge a fixed admin fee for holding a trade overnight, either after a few days or from the first day. Some widen the spread a little, and some charge no admin fee at all. Not every broker works the same way, so read your broker's terms before opening an account. Module 4 covers broker and account types in detail.

Why the total is negative (the shovel sellers)

A fee is cut on every trade. So if you add up the profit and loss of all traders, the total is not zero: it is minus. Think of a cake where one slice is always cut away as a fee before anyone eats. The people who earn whether the market goes up or down are brokers, banks and signal sellers. In a gold rush, the one who earns most is the one selling shovels.

That is why regulated brokers in Europe and the UK must publish a risk warning on their own websites, and those warnings typically say about 60% to 80% of their retail accounts lose money trading CFDs.

The truth about a $50 or $100 account

Say you risk 2% of your account on each trade. On $100 that is $2, on $50 just $1. If a good trader makes 5% in a whole month, which is a very good result and not guaranteed, that is $5 on $100 and $2.50 on $50.

AccountRisk per tradeMost you lose on one tradeA very good month (+5%)
$502%$1.00$2.50
$1002%$2.00$5.00
$5003%$15.00$25.00
$1,0001%$10.00$50.00
$10,0001%$100.00$500.00

Can this run a household? No. This is where people go wrong: $5 feels too small, so they put 20% or 30% on one trade, and a few trades later the account is gone. A small account is for learning, not for earning.

How much should you risk per trade?

Risk means: if this trade goes wrong, how much of your account goes. You control it with a stop loss and the right lot size (Module 8 covers it fully; you can already try the free lot size calculator). A practical rule:

  • Small account ($50–$500): 2–3% per trade is acceptable, because the amount is small anyway and it is a learning account.
  • Bigger account: 1% or less, because every percent is now a big amount. 1% of $10,000 is $100.

10 losing trades in a row: 1% vs 3% vs 20% risk

Ten losses in a row can happen to any trader. Here is what it does to the account:

Risk per tradeAccount after 10 lossesTotal drawdown
1%$904.38−9.6%
3%$737.42−26.3%
20%$107.37−89.3%

At 1% you can recover. At 20% the account is practically finished (read more about drawdown and recovery).

Is forex trading profitable?

Yes, but only for traders who manage risk. That means three things: before every trade you decide the most you can lose, you have a daily and weekly loss limit, and you trade a tested plan. In the market, the one who earns is the one who survives first. Protect first, then earn.

How do you make money from forex trading?

From the price difference: you buy a pair and it rises, or sell and it falls. The money comes from the losses of other traders and from players who trade for their needs, such as companies and central banks. After fees the total of all traders is negative, so only traders with better decisions and strict risk control end up in profit.
Is forex trading profitable?

It can be, but most retail traders lose. Regulated brokers' own risk warnings typically say about 60% to 80% of retail CFD accounts lose money. Profit is possible only with a tested plan, a fixed risk per trade and daily and weekly loss limits.
Can I make money in forex with $100?
You can learn with $100, but not earn a living. At 2% risk you lose at most $2 per trade, and a very good month of +5% is about $5. A small account is a learning account.
Where does the money lost in forex go?

To four places: fees (spread, commission and swap), the broker itself when it takes the other side of your trade, better traders and institutions, and, outside the market, scams and paid signal sellers.
How much should I risk per trade?

On a small learning account of about $50 to $500, 2–3% per trade is acceptable. On a bigger account keep it at 1% or less. After 10 losses in a row, 1% risk costs about 9.6% of the account, 20% risk costs about 89%.
Is forex a zero-sum game?

Before costs, roughly yes: money moves from one hand to another. After the spread, commission and swap are taken out, the total of all traders is negative, which is why brokers, banks and signal sellers earn whichever way the market moves.
Do Islamic swap-free accounts have no cost?

They have no swap, but most brokers charge a fixed admin fee for holding trades overnight, either after a few days or from the first day, and some widen the spread. Terms differ, so read your broker's conditions.

lessons.notes:
"Guaranteed profit"? Stop for a second

If someone tells you "just follow my signal, there is no chance of loss, guaranteed profit every month", stop for a second. You may not be about to learn trading; you may be about to walk into someone's trap. The most dangerous part: at the start they can even show you profit, to win your trust and get you to put in more. Then one day your screen shows $5,000 profit, you press Withdraw, and the reply comes: "First pay the tax."

This lesson shows the 5 steps that almost every forex trading scam goes through, plus a hidden 6th step, so that you can recognise the next message in ten seconds. The last part explains what to do if you have already been caught.

Where does a forex scammer make money?

Forex trading is trading on the rise and fall of currency prices. It carries risk, and there is no guarantee of profit. But on Facebook, WhatsApp, Telegram and Instagram some people sell it as if doubling your money were one button away. In Lesson 0.2 we saw the 4 places losers' money goes, and one of them was outside the market. This lesson opens that place.

A scammer does not earn from the market. He earns from you:

  • the fee for a "VIP" signal group;
  • a commission for opening your account with an unregulated B-book broker (a broker that takes the other side of your trade itself);
  • your deposit, collected in the name of "account management";
  • and at the end, fake fees on withdrawal.

Whether the market goes up or down, his income is fixed. And this is not a small problem: Pakistan's cybercrime agency NCCIA received more than 150,000 complaints in 2025, about 82,000 of them about financial fraud.

The 5 steps of a forex scam

StepWhat you seeThe red flag
1. The bait"5% profit every day", "account doubled every week", "no loss"Any guaranteed or fixed profit
2. TrustFree signals for a few days, only winning screenshots, cars, cash, hotel roomsNo full history with losses
3. Pressure"Only 10 seats left", "offer ends tonight", "deposit now or miss the next signal"No time given to think or verify
4. Your money in their hands"Open with our broker", "give us your login", "send money to our account"Unregulated broker, shared login, personal account
5. The trapProfit keeps rising on a dashboard; a big withdrawal needs "tax", an "unlock fee" or "one more deposit"Any fee to get your own money out

Step 1: the bait (guaranteed profit)

A message, an ad or a video promises a fixed return. In Lesson 0.2 we did the maths: $100 growing 10% a day would, in a year, be more than all the wealth in the world. So a promise of guaranteed or fixed profit is not proof; it is the first red flag. Regulators such as the US CFTC and the UK FCA list it as the most common sign of an investment scam. And if someone says "there is risk in trading, but not in my signals", that is still a guarantee in different words.

Step 2: trust (free signals and screenshots)

A few free signals win, and the group posts only the winning screenshots, next to expensive cars and stacks of notes. A screenshot does not tell you how many trades lost, how much was risked, or how much money was in the account before. Ask one direct question: where is the full history, including losses, that an independent third party can verify? If the answer is vague, or every question gets a new screenshot, stop. Module 12 of this course has a separate lesson on how fake screenshots are made.

Step 3: pressure ("join now")

Countdowns and "last chance" messages exist so that you do not get time to think and check. Your simple rule: if you are not given time to understand an offer, do not send money to it. A good decision is not spoiled by waiting one night. A scammer wants exactly that you do not wait.

Step 4: your money in their hands

You are told to open an account with "their" broker, which is often unregulated, to hand over your login so they can trade for you, or to send money straight to their account. Remember two things. First, a link, logo or certificate posted in a group is not proof: scammers copy real companies' names and even registration numbers, and build look-alike websites with one letter changed in the address. Second, never send trading money to a person's private account. How to recognise a regulated broker is covered in Module 4 (and in our forex brokers guide).

Step 5: the trap (fees on withdrawal)

The profit on the dashboard keeps growing. Some fake platforms even let you withdraw a small amount at the start, so that you invest more. Pakistan's SECP has warned that such apps show a fake balance and fake profit on a fake dashboard while no real trading takes place at all. Then, when you try to take out a large amount: pay tax first, pay an account unlock fee, deposit a little more, and then you will get everything. This is the biggest red flag of all. At this point do not send a single rupee more.

The hidden 6th step: the recovery scam

After a scam, someone contacts you: "I will get your stuck money back, just pay a fee first." According to the UK regulator FCA, these "recovery room" callers are often the same people who ran the first scam, or people who bought your details. No genuine government body asks for a fee to recover your money.

5 checks before you send money to any offer

Each check breaks one step of the scam:

  1. Stop at the word "guarantee". High profit with no risk is a red flag (breaks step 1).
  2. Ask for the loss record. Winning screenshots alone do not tell the whole story (step 2).
  3. Never deposit in a hurry. Do not decide under pressure, countdowns or "last chance" (step 3).
  4. Verify the firm yourself. Check its name, website and contact details on the regulator's official website; do not trust a link sent in a group (step 4).
  5. Keep your account and money in your own control. Never share your password, OTP or account access, and never risk more than you can afford to lose (step 5). See risk management.

These steps do not remove every risk, but they let you see the traps in front of you.

Already sent money? Do this now

Do not blame yourself; act quickly:

  • Do not pay any more deposits or fees.
  • Save screenshots of chats, receipts and transaction details.
  • Inform your bank or wallet immediately.
  • Complain to your country's financial regulator or cybercrime channel: in Pakistan the NCCIA helpline 1799 (nccia.gov.pk), in India the cyber fraud helpline 1930 (cybercrime.gov.in).
  • If you shared a password or login, change it at once.

There is no guarantee you will get the money back, but the sooner you report, the better the chance.

Forex trading: real or fake?

Forex itself is real: it is the world's biggest market, and profit is possible. But a promise of guaranteed profit is an alarm bell. Read more in Is forex a scam? and our guide to forex signal groups.

  1. Take any "profit" message or ad that has reached your phone.
  2. Count how many of today's 5 steps you can see in it, out of 5.

Write your answer in the YouTube comments, and share this lesson with a friend or family member it could save from a scam. Next lesson: binary options, and why they are not forex. If you missed it, start with Lesson 0.1: the course roadmap, or see the full syllabus.

Is forex trading a scam?

No. Forex is a real market and the biggest in the world, but it carries real risk and most retail traders lose. What is a scam is anyone who promises guaranteed or fixed profit, sells "no loss" signals, or asks you to pay a fee before you can withdraw.
How do fake forex signal groups work?

They usually follow 5 steps: the bait (guaranteed profit), trust (a few free signals and only winning screenshots), pressure ("only 10 seats left"), getting your money into their hands (their broker, your login or a personal account), and the trap (profit on a dashboard that can't be withdrawn without paying a "tax" or "unlock fee").
Why do they ask for tax or an unlock fee before withdrawal?

Because the balance and profit on a fake platform are not real. The "tax" or "unlock fee" is simply more money for the scammer. A genuine broker takes any fees from your account balance; it does not ask you to send new money to release your own. Do not send another rupee.
Can a recovery agent get my scammed money back?

Be very careful. The UK FCA warns that people who call offering to recover scam losses for a fee are often the same scammers or people who bought your details. No genuine government body charges a fee to recover your money. Report to your bank and your country's cybercrime channel instead.

60 seconds, one question

A binary options app asks you a single question: will the price of Gold, a currency pair or something else be higher or lower after a fixed time? Right, and a Rs 1,000 stake pays Rs 800 profit. Wrong, and the whole Rs 1,000 is gone. It sounds simple. But if you are right exactly 5 times out of 10, why does the account keep shrinking? This lesson opens that calculation, and shows why these apps are not forex at all.

What is binary trading (binary options)?

Binary means two. There are only two possible results: yes or no. You do three things:

  • choose a direction, UP or DOWN (sometimes called Higher/Lower or Call/Put);
  • choose an amount;
  • choose a time: 30 seconds, 1 minute or 5 minutes. A countdown timer starts.

When the timer ends, the decision is made. If price closed even one point in your favour, you get the fixed payout (for example 80% of your stake). If it closed even one point against you, you lose the entire stake. How far price moved does not matter; only which side of your entry it was on in the last second. That is why binary options are called all or nothing.

Binary options vs forex trading: the real difference

Binary optionsForex trading
Your decisionUp or down onlyBuy or sell a currency pair
ResultFixed payout or lose the whole stakeProfit or loss grows with how far price moves
Stop loss / take profitNoneYou set both in advance
Closing the tradeA timer decidesYou close whenever you want
Who is on the other sideOften the app itselfThe market, through a regulated broker
PakistanNo platform is licensed; illegalLegal through PMEX-licensed brokers

In forex the control is in your hands: a stop loss caps the loss, a take profit locks in profit, and there is no timer over your head. In binary, price can be in your favour the whole minute and flip in the last second, and you still lose. Pips, leverage, margin and broker types come in later lessons (what is a pip, what is leverage).

Binary trading math: why 5 wins out of 10 still lose

Say every trade is Rs 100 and the payout is 80%. A win pays Rs 80; a loss costs the full Rs 100. You take 10 trades and win exactly half, like tossing a coin:

TradesCalculationResult
5 wins5 × Rs 80+Rs 400
5 losses5 × Rs 100-Rs 500
Net-Rs 100

To simply break even you need a win rate of 100 ÷ (100 + 80) = 55.6%, about 6 out of every 10 trades, and that is only breaking even, not profit. Being right 6 times in 10, again and again, on one-minute moves that are pushed around by news, spread and noise is extremely hard. So when someone claims "99% accuracy", ask: on how many trades was it tested? Were the losses shown too, or only winning screenshots? Many people also double the next trade after a loss to win it back; that martingale habit empties the account even faster.

Who is on the other side of your trade?

In forex your order meets the market price. In binary apps your trade is often made with the app itself: when you pick UP, the app is on the other side. That means when you lose, the app earns, and when you win, the app pays. And the payout maths you just saw is set in the app's favour from the start. When the UK Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) banned binary options, it described them as gambling products dressed up as financial instruments.

Is binary trading legal? What regulators did

  • Europe: ESMA banned the sale of binary options to retail clients from 2 July 2018; national regulators then made permanent rules.
  • UK: the FCA made the ban permanent from 2 April 2019.
  • India: the RBI says binary trading is not permitted in forex, and many well-known binary apps are on the RBI Alert List of unauthorised platforms. The list is not complete, so an app being missing from it is not proof that it is allowed.
  • Pakistan: no binary options platform is licensed by the SECP. In April 2025 the SECP warned the public that offshore trading platforms offering forex, commodities and options without regulatory approval are illegal.

So the straight answer: binary option brokers are illegal in Pakistan. Never open an account with them. They are not legal and they are not real trading. Treat them like gambling apps whose business runs on your losses.

Forex is a real business

Forex, by contrast, is the world's largest currency market, where banks, companies and countries exchange currencies every day (what is forex trading). In Pakistan forex is legal with regulated brokers: through brokers licensed by PMEX, the exchange regulated by the SECP. How to check that a broker is really regulated comes in Module 4 (meanwhile see forex brokers in Pakistan and forex trading in Pakistan and India).

How to recognise a binary app in 10 seconds

These apps often sell themselves as "forex" or "trading", so do not go by the name; look at the screen.

Binary app screenReal forex platform (MT4/MT5)
Higher / Lower, Up / Down, Call / PutBuy and Sell
Fixed time trade, countdown timer, expiryNo timer
Payout 80-90%Lot size, spread
No stop loss boxStop loss and take profit boxes

Watch the ad lines too: "one-minute strategy", "earn Rs 5,000 a day", "99% accuracy", and YouTube videos that show only winning trades with an app link below. That link is often an affiliate link: the more you lose, the more commission the person sharing it earns (see how forex scams work).

Practical task

Open any trading ad on your phone. Without installing the app and without depositing anything, ask three questions:

  1. Am I only being asked to choose up or down?
  2. Is there a timer of a few seconds or minutes?
  3. Is a payout % written, and can the whole stake be lost if I am wrong?

If most answers are yes, it is binary options. Stop right there.

lessons.notes:
What is forex?

Forex comes from two English words: foreign and exchange. It means changing the currency of one country into the currency of another. When someone in Pakistan buys US dollars, when a company in India buys euros to import a machine from Europe, or when a tourist changes money into dirhams in Dubai, that is forex.

Forex trading means buying or selling a currency with the aim of profiting from a change in its price.

How big is the forex market?

According to the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) Triennial Survey, about $9.6 trillion worth of currencies changed hands every day in April 2025. That is why forex is called the largest financial market in the world. It has no single building: banks and institutions around the world are linked by computers, and the market runs 24 hours a day, five days a week (see the market timings in Pakistan and India).

A simple example: the money changer

Ahmed buys 100 US dollars from a money changer at Rs 280 per dollar and pays Rs 28,000. A few days later the dollar rises to Rs 285. He sells the same 100 dollars and receives Rs 28,500: a profit of Rs 500.

If the dollar had fallen to Rs 276, he would have received Rs 27,600: a loss of Rs 400. This is the whole idea behind forex trading: profit or loss from the difference in price. (The numbers are only an example.)

Rate100 USD in rupeesResult
BuyRs 280Rs 28,000-
Sell if the dollar risesRs 285Rs 28,500+Rs 500
Sell if the dollar fallsRs 276Rs 27,600-Rs 400

Why do currency prices change?

Because of demand and supply. When many people and companies want dollars and there are few dollars available, the dollar becomes expensive. When there are plenty of dollars and few buyers, it becomes cheaper. Demand is moved by interest rates, inflation, economic news and world events. Each of these gets its own lesson later in the series.

How online forex trading works

Today most forex trading happens online. You do not hold the dollars in your hand: through a broker, on a platform such as MT5 on your computer or phone, you trade on the price going up or down.

  • Currencies are always quoted in pairs, for example the euro against the US dollar, written EUR/USD.
  • If EUR/USD rises from 1.1000 to 1.1050, the euro has become stronger against the dollar.
  • Not only currencies: Gold is traded too, as XAU/USD.
  • Pips, lots and spread come in the next lessons.

The honest truth about risk

Forex is not a job and not a get-rich-quick scheme. Price differences make losses just as easily as profits. Many regulated brokers state on their own websites that most of their retail clients' accounts lose money. The usual reason is trading without learning, without a plan and with too much risk. Anyone who promises "guaranteed profit" or "fixed daily income" is showing the biggest red flag (read about signal scams).

Is forex trading legal?

The rules are different in every country. In India, for example, the Reserve Bank of India allows residents to trade forex only through authorised persons and on recognised exchanges, for permitted purposes. Before you start anything, check the official rules of your own country. Our guide to forex trading in Pakistan and India explains the details.

The most common beginner mistake

Watching two videos, or taking someone's signal, and putting real money in on the first day. The right path is: learn first, practise on a demo account, make your own plan, then start small. This whole series follows that path.

Practical task (10 minutes)

  1. Note today's US dollar rate in rupees from a bank's website. Check it again after three days and write down who gained from the change: the person who bought dollars or the person who sold them?
  2. Write one line: "Why do I want to learn forex?" Share your answer in the YouTube comments.

How big is the forex market?

The Bank for International Settlements (BIS), the bank of the world's central banks, counts global currency trading every three years. Its April 2025 Triennial Survey found about $9.6 trillion traded every day, around 28% more than in 2022. To feel that number: counting one dollar every second, just one trillion would take more than 31,000 years.

That figure is not just people trading on mobile apps. It has three big parts:

PartShare of daily turnoverWhat it is
FX swapsabout 42%Banks and institutions exchange one currency for another for a period, for their own funding needs
Spotabout 31% (around $3 trillion a day)Exchange right now, at today's price. The price on your chart comes from the spot market
Outright forwardsabout 19%Companies fix today a rate for a future date

So most of the market exists to move real payments and to manage currency risk. Not every deal is a trader's bet. One currency is everywhere: the US dollar is on one side of about 89% of all trades, and EUR/USD alone is about 21% of the market.

Where does forex trade? No building: the OTC market

Shares are easy to picture. The Pakistan Stock Exchange has a building in Karachi: like one big vegetable market, everyone goes there and everyone gets one rate. Forex is the opposite. Picture thousands of shops across a city, all connected by phone. You can buy from any of them, and each shop's rate is very close to the others, but not exactly the same.

This is called an OTC (over-the-counter) market: deals happen directly between two parties, not through one central exchange. Banks, institutions and companies are linked by computer networks. That is why forex has no single official price, and no one country or person can close it.

Some cities are still the heart of the network. According to the BIS, London handles about 38% of global FX trading, New York 19%, Singapore about 12% and Hong Kong 7%: together about 75%. They sit in different time zones, so the market keeps running through the working week (see the market timings in Pakistan and India).

Who trades forex? The market pyramid

  1. Central banks such as the State Bank of Pakistan and the US Federal Reserve. They do not trade for profit: they manage reserves and the currency, and one decision can move the whole market.
  2. Big dealer banks: about 47% of turnover is between these banks. They quote buy and sell prices all day.
  3. Other financial institutions: smaller banks, hedge funds, pension funds, investment companies and brokers, about 48%.
  4. Companies that import and export: surprisingly, only about 5%.
  5. Retail traders, you and me, reaching the market through a broker. In this ocean our trade is one drop.

Why do they trade? Payments, hedging and speculation

Every player has a different reason. A Pakistani company importing a machine from Japan must pay in yen, so it sells rupees to buy yen. A textile exporter paid in dollars sells those dollars for rupees. A Pakistani working abroad sends money home, and his dollars become rupees.

A company afraid that the rate will move against it in three months fixes the rate today. That is hedging: not profit, protection. A trader who buys or sells only to profit from the price difference is doing speculation, which is what most retail traders do. Remember that the people on the other side usually have far more money, information and technology than you. The smart way is to swim with the big fish, not against them.

How is the price made?

No one person and no one bank sets the price. Every moment thousands of buyers and sellers make their offers, and the price at which a buyer and a seller agree becomes the price of that moment. If importers need more dollars and sellers are few, sellers ask more and the dollar rises. If remittances and exports bring plenty of dollars and buyers are few, the dollar gets cheaper. These buying and selling decisions change with news: interest rates, inflation, jobs data and central bank decisions. Each candle on your chart is a picture of this tug of war. The small gap between the buy and sell price is the spread.

Pakistan: interbank rate vs open market rate

Pakistan has followed a market-based, flexible exchange rate since 1999. The dollar's rate is formed by demand and supply in the market between banks, the interbank market, while the State Bank manages reserves and supervises. When you buy dollars from an exchange company in the bazaar you get a second rate, the open market rate. In July 2026, for example, the open market dollar was around Rs 279 while the interbank rate was about Rs 1.5 lower.

When this gap grows too wide people look for illegal channels, which is why both the State Bank and the IMF want it kept small. One currency, two places, two rates: that is the real face of the forex market.

Where does your forex trade go? The money changer example

Think of the money changer in your local bazaar. You walk into an exchange company's shop and buy dollars. Your deal is with the shopkeeper: you pay him and you get dollars from him. You do not need to know where he got them. But behind him there is a system: he buys from a bigger dealer, and the big dealer buys from banks.

Forex works the same way, only online and in a fraction of a second. In forex the shopkeeper is your broker, and your deal is with the broker. Technically you open a contract called a CFD (contract for difference): you are not taking euro notes home, you trade on the price going up or down. The broker gets its prices from liquidity providers (LPs): big banks and financial companies that quote buy and sell rates all the time. Behind the LPs is the interbank market we met in Lesson 1.2.

What happens after you click Buy in MT5: the journey in 6 steps

  1. Order slip. MT5 prepares a small order on your phone: the pair (EURUSD), Buy or Sell, the volume (say 0.10 lot), and your stop loss and take profit if you set them.
  2. Internet and ping. The slip travels to the broker's trade server, usually in a data centre in London or New York. The travel time is called ping, in milliseconds; desktop MT5 shows it in the bottom-right corner.
  3. Server check. Like a shopkeeper checking the customer has enough money, the server checks: is the account OK, is the market open for this pair, is the lot size within limits, and is there enough free margin?
  4. Best rate from many LPs. A broker is connected to several LPs, and each streams a slightly different rate every moment. The broker's bridge (aggregator) looks at all of them: a Buy goes to the LP with the lowest Ask, a Sell to the LP with the highest Bid.
  5. The deal is done. Either the bridge sends the order straight to an LP (A-Book), or the broker completes the deal inside its own system (B-Book). On your screen the result looks the same: the trade is open.
  6. Confirmation. The confirmation comes back to your phone: the position appears in the Trade tab with a ticket number, open price and volume, and your margin is locked. The whole journey usually takes less than one second.

Remember five words: click, check, rate, deal, confirmation.

The margin check, with real numbers

ItemValue
TradeBuy 0.10 lot EURUSD
Contract size10,000 euros
Value at 1.1011about $11,011
Leverage1:100

If your free margin is less than the margin needed, the order stops at the server and MT5 shows Not enough money. Leverage and margin are explained fully in Module 3 (what is leverage?).

Market execution and slippage: 1.1010 becomes 1.1011

Say the Ask on your screen was 1.1010 when you pressed Buy. By the time the order arrived, nobody was selling at 1.1010 anymore, and the nearest rate available across all LPs was 1.1011. Your order fills there. This is market execution: the order does not stop, it fills at the best rate available at that moment. The difference between your click price and your fill price is slippage. Normally it is zero or tiny; during big news it can be larger, and sometimes it is even in your favour.

Why a new trade starts with a small minus

You buy at the Ask, but a buy closes at the Bid. The gap between them is the spread, so right after opening your trade shows a small loss. On every new tick the profit or loss changes. Closing a buy means selling at the Bid: the same journey runs in reverse, the result is added to your balance and the margin is free again.

A-BookB-Book

Most big brokers today run both together, the hybrid model. Both are legitimate business methods. As a trader your job is to check that the broker is regulated, so a government regulator watches its systems and accounts.

How forex brokers make money

Like the money changer's board with one rate to buy and another to sell, every pair in MT5 has a Bid (where you sell) and an Ask (where you buy). The difference is the spread. Some accounts have a very small spread but charge a commission per lot. Whatever it is called, it is the cost of your business, like a shop's rent. Check the spread before you trade, especially around news, when it can widen for a while.

Is your money safe? Three things to check

  1. Regulation: a licence from a reputable regulator, checked on the regulator's own website.
  2. Segregated accounts: client money kept apart from the company's own money.
  3. Negative balance protection: offered by many regulated brokers, so your loss cannot go beyond your deposit.

The full checklist comes in Module 4; meanwhile read how to choose a forex broker and forex brokers in Pakistan.

How do forex brokers work?

A forex broker connects you to the market. When you click Buy or Sell, the broker's server checks your account and margin, then its bridge takes the best price from several liquidity providers and either passes the order to an LP (A-Book) or completes it internally (B-Book). The confirmation returns to your platform, usually in under a second.
What is a liquidity provider in forex?

A liquidity provider (LP) is a large bank or financial company that continuously quotes buy and sell prices to brokers. A broker connects to several LPs and routes a buy to the lowest Ask and a sell to the highest Bid.
Why did my order fill at a different price?

With market execution the order fills at the best price available when it reaches the server. If the price moved between your click and the fill, for example from 1.1010 to 1.1011, the difference is slippage. It is usually zero or tiny and can be larger during big news.
How do forex brokers make money?
Mainly from the spread, the gap between the Bid and Ask, and on some accounts a commission per lot. B-Book brokers can also earn from the net result of client trades they keep in-house.
Is my money safe with a forex broker?
Choose a broker licensed by a reputable regulator (check on the regulator's own website), that keeps client money in segregated accounts and offers negative balance protection.

lessons.notes:
What is a currency code? ISO 4217 in one minute

Every currency in the world has a three-letter code set by the global standard ISO 4217. Banks, airline tickets and MT5 all use the same codes so there is no confusion. The usual pattern: the first two letters are the country and the third is the currency: USD (United States + Dollar), PKR (Pakistan + Rupee), INR (India + Rupee), JPY (Japan + Yen), GBP (Great Britain + Pound), AUD, CAD and NZD.

It is a pattern, not a formula. CHF is the Swiss franc, from the Latin name Confoederatio Helvetica. EUR is shared by many European countries, so it is built from EU. Gold is XAU and silver XAG: X means not a country's currency, and Au is gold's chemical symbol from the Latin aurum. That is why gold in MT5 is XAUUSD.

Many brokers add a suffix such as EURUSDm, EURUSD.pro or EURUSD.ecn. The real pair is always the first six letters; the ending usually shows the account type. Right-click the symbol and open Specification to see the full details.

Base currency and quote currency: the petrol pump example

In forex you never buy one currency alone; you always buy one against another, so two codes are written together as a currency pair. The first is the base currency and the second is the quote currency.

A petrol pump board says: 1 litre = 250 rupees (for example). The litre is always one; the rupees show its price. A pair works the same way: in EURUSD 1.1011 the euro is the litre (always 1) and the dollar is the rupees. So the number is the price of one euro in dollars.

Common mistake: is 1.1011 the dollar's price?

No. In Pakistan we hear "the dollar is 276", so the mind thinks every number is the dollar's price. In forex language that is USDPKR 276: the dollar is first, so 276 is the dollar's price in rupees. In EURUSD 1.1011 the euro is first, so 1.1011 is the euro's price in dollars: one euro is about one dollar and ten cents, and with one dollar you will not get a full euro.

How to read any currency pair in 3 steps

  1. Say the first currency with the word one.
  2. Say equals.
  3. Say the screen number with the second currency.

EURUSD 1.1011: one euro equals 1.1011 dollars. GBPUSD 1.27: one pound equals 1.27 dollars. USDJPY 150: one dollar equals 150 yen (here the dollar is first, so the number is the dollar's price).

What Buy and Sell really mean

Buying EURUSD means buying euros and selling dollars; you expect the euro to strengthen against the dollar. Selling EURUSD means selling euros and buying dollars. The Buy or Sell decision is always about the base currency. If the chart goes up, the base currency is getting stronger: EURUSD from 1.1011 to 1.1050 means one euro now buys more dollars; down to 1.0980 means the euro got cheaper. Profit or loss also depends on spread and lot size, which we calculate in Module 2.

The rule: is the dollar on the left or the right?

When news says the dollar is getting stronger: in EURUSD the dollar is on the right (quote), so the pair goes down. In USDJPY the dollar is on the left (base), so the pair goes up. One news, two pairs, opposite directions. Always check where the dollar sits before you trade on dollar news.

Major, minor and exotic currency pairs

  • Major pairs: the US dollar against one of the strongest currencies. Usually seven: EURUSD, USDJPY, GBPUSD, USDCHF, AUDUSD, USDCAD, NZDUSD. The dollar is on one side of about 89% of all trades, and in the BIS 2025 survey EURUSD alone was about 21% of the market, USDJPY about 14% and GBPUSD about 8%. More buyers and sellers mean lower spreads.
  • Minor (cross) pairs: no dollar, but both currencies are big: EURGBP, EURJPY, GBPJPY, AUDCAD. Spreads are a bit higher, and GBPJPY is famous for fast moves ("the Beast").
  • Exotic pairs: one big currency plus one from an emerging or small economy: USDTRY, USDZAR, USDMXN. USDPKR and USDINR also belong here, but most brokers do not offer them. Few buyers and sellers mean wide spreads, sudden moves and higher swap.

Road analogy: majors are the motorway (heavy, smooth traffic, small toll), minors are city roads (rush and bumps), exotics are a village dirt road (few cars, potholes).

The family test

Memorise eight currencies: USD, EUR, JPY, GBP, CHF, AUD, CAD, NZD. If a pair has a currency outside these eight, it is exotic. If both are inside, check for the dollar: dollar = major, no dollar = minor. AUDUSD = major, EURJPY = minor, USDTRY = exotic. Brokers draw these lines slightly differently, and spreads change with the broker, account type and time of day.

Which currency pairs should a beginner trade?

Start with one or two majors such as EURUSD: low spread, smoother movement, and learning material everywhere. But no pair is safe: a low spread only means a lower cost. Before any trade, check the spread at your broker, check market activity, practise on demo, and decide your maximum loss first. In MT5, right-click Market Watch and open Symbols: most brokers keep Majors, Minors and Exotics in separate folders, where you can compare their spreads.
